title: Ang 175–200: Guru Arjan in Gauri
hookLine: the fifth Guru's many Gauri hymns
tomorrow: how do you trust a seed you can't see?

cards: Somebody in every group chat has the line: once I get the car, the job, the apartment, then I'll finally be okay. Simran said it this morning, about the old pickup her dad promised her if she passes the test.

Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, opens his long run of Gauri hymns on Ang 175 with that exact question turned around: how does well-being come, brother? And his list of where it doesn't come from starts with the palace.

teach.h: NOT IN THE MANSION, NOT IN THE ARMY.
teach.b: Here's the hymn, in paraphrase. Well-being isn't in a house full of wealth, or lofty mansions with lovely shade.
A man delights in elephants and horses, gathers armies and servants, and the noose of ego tightens at his neck.

teach.h: A KING WHO'S A BEGGAR IN A DREAM.
teach.b: He rules in all ten directions, and it's like a king who turns beggar in a dream.

Then the turn: the True Guru showed me one well-being, that whatever the Lord does, the devotee accepts with love; ego dies, and the self settles. So what is the hymn asking? Sikh readers hear it two ways.
One reading: let go. The list is a warning; the noose is real, and the safe heart holds things very loosely, ready to walk away.

teach.h: ANOTHER: THE LEANING, NOT THE HAVING.
teach.b: The other reading: it's the leaning, not the having. Sikh teaching honors the householder's life: working, earning, raising a family, sharing.
On this reading the hymn never says don't own a horse; it says don't expect the horse to hold you up. Notice where they agree.
Neither thinks the palace delivers peace. Both put kusal, well-being, in the same place: a heart that has stopped insisting. They differ on how far from the palace you walk to find it.

how: Guru Arjan's Gauri hymns are sung as kirtan in the gurdwara; Sikh teaching pairs them with the householder's life of honest work and sharing, and readers discuss how far detachment should go.

o: the page where Guru Arjan's long run of Gauri hymns begins
the last page Guru Nanak wrote in the raga Gauri
a hymn of the fifth Guru on giving away all wealth

games.q: where well-being isn't — tap the pairs.
p: a noose of ego at the neck

s: Ang 175 says owning a house or a horse is wrong
it says well-being isn't found there; readers differ on how far to let go.
the hymn's answer is a heart that accepts what the Lord does
the one well-being the True Guru showed.
Sikh readers all agree the hymn means give everything up
some hear let go; others hear stop leaning, honoring the householder's life.

games.q: Maya reads the hymn and says, "so wanting the truck is wrong." you lean the other way. what's the strongest case for her reading?
o: the noose line is serious: what you lean on can tie you, so hold it loosely.
the hymn names houses and horses, so owning them must be banned.
it's about kings, so it says nothing to an ordinary teenager.
games.why: the best case for 'let go' is the hymn's own noose: what you lean on can tighten. both readings agree the truck won't bring well-being.

practice: Count three things you have that once felt like the thing that would fix everything: a phone, a room, a friend, a skill. For each, notice what it gave you, and what it couldn't.
Then rest in whatever is left over when the list is done.
